notes.meaning: Jeroboam broke the northern tribes away from the royal family of David and led them into idol worship. He set up golden calves and stopped the people from traveling to God's temple in Jerusalem. This rebellion started a long chain of evil that dragged the nation down.

The people of Israel clung to the false worship Jeroboam had begun and refused to change. Generation after generation followed the same bad example instead of returning to the true God. Their hearts remained stubborn despite all of God's warnings through the prophets.

God finally sent the Israelites away into captivity in Assyria, just as His prophets had warned. He removed them from His land and His special care because of their unfaithfulness. The northern kingdom was scattered and never returned as an independent nation.

The Assyrian empire moved captive peoples from Babylon and other regions into the empty towns of Samaria. By shuffling conquered groups around, the Assyrians aimed to stop rebellions and break national loyalties. These new foreign settlers took over the land and made its towns their home.

At first, the new settlers did not worship the Lord at all. God allowed wild lions to enter their towns and attack them as a sign of judgment. Even though they were foreigners, God showed that the land belonged to Him and demanded reverence.

The settlers sent a message to the king of Assyria explaining their plight. Like many ancient peoples, they believed every region belonged to a local god who needed proper rituals to stay peaceful. They realized they were suffering because they did not know how to worship the God of this land.

The king of Assyria ordered that an exiled priest be sent back to Samaria to teach the settlers. The king cared about keeping order and stopping the lion attacks rather than honoring the true God. The priest's job was simply to train the people in the local religious customs.

One of the exiled priests came back and settled at Bethel to teach the new residents how to worship the Lord. Because Bethel had been the center of Jeroboam's golden-calf shrines, this priest likely taught a flawed, compromised faith. Even so, the people learned some outward forms of worshiping the God of Israel.

The settlers accepted what they were taught about the Lord, but they did not give up their ancestral idols. Instead, each group made images of its own gods and placed them in the local shrines across the countryside. They mixed the worship of the true God with their own pagan practices.

People from each conquered city set up their own special deities. The settlers from Sepharvaim committed the worst evil by burning their own children in sacrificial fires. These terrible customs brought deep corruption into the towns of Samaria.

The new residents began offering sacrifices to the Lord, but they picked ordinary people from any background to serve as priests. They copied Jeroboam's old shortcut instead of following God's rule that only Aaron's family could serve at the altar. Their worship was built on convenience rather than God's law.

The settlers tried to have it both ways by fearing the Lord while still serving their own pagan gods. They showed outward respect to God to avoid the lions, but their hearts belonged to their traditional idols. This kind of mixed religion is called syncretism, which combines true faith with false beliefs.

The writer explains that continuing these mixed customs meant the people did not truly worship the Lord at all. True reverence means obeying God's written laws and serving Him alone. Outward ceremonies mixed with idolatry fail to meet God's standard.

God had made a sacred covenant with Israel, which was a special binding agreement with clear promises and duties. He commanded His people never to bow down to any false gods. Instead, they were to worship only the Lord, who had rescued them from slavery in Egypt with His great power.

The Lord gave written commandments and laws so His people would never forget their duty to Him. He promised that if they trusted and worshiped Him alone, He would protect them from all their enemies. Real security comes from full devotion to God, not from seeking help from idols.

The people refused to listen to God's clear commands and stayed trapped in their old habits. They chose familiar idolatry over wholehearted obedience to the living God. Their refusal showed how deeply rooted false worship had become.

The chapter closes by noting that this split religion was passed down from parents to children over many generations. The settlers and their descendants claimed to honor the Lord while still serving their carved statues. Halfhearted devotion created a spiritual confusion that lasted for centuries.
